name: Colin Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, so no links to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and we're not selling anything. What you say here is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the cardboard box plant down by the canal, the corrugator end of it. I run a rotary die-cutter, which is basically a big drum with blades that punches the shapes out of the flat board, so the boxes can be folded later. I feed it, keep the stacks straight, knock out the scrap, change the cutting dies when the job changes, and I'm still slow at the changeovers, a good forty minutes when the lads do it in twenty-five. Two years in, so I'm still the new boy, even at 43.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What were you doing before that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Warehouse, loading lorries for sixteen years, until my back went. The doctor said no more lifting all day, so I took this, which has a lot less lifting but more thinking than I'm used to. I don't mind it. It's steady, it's indoors, and Tess likes that I come home in one piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, another thing that was going to change everything and didn't. Like those self-checkouts that never work. I'm not online much, so I'd just say it in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job and get a bit faster at the changeovers, which is all I'm after. I don't like big changes, I've had enough of them with my back. So that suits me down to the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Same shift, same machine. Keep the bit of savings we've got, about two months, maybe three, and keep chipping at the mortgage like we always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Relieved, maybe, but mostly just normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any of these AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My lad Ryan uses something on his phone for his homework, and Tess has asked it a recipe once. I've never seen the point, I'd rather ask a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the job better in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better seats in the canteen, honestly. And getting my changeovers down to half an hour, so Mick stops looking at his watch at me.

S0.say: Another thing that was going to change everything didn't, like the self-checkouts that never work. He'd say it in the canteen, since he's hardly online.
S0.think: He keeps his job and slowly gets faster at changeovers, which is all he wants. After his back injury he's had enough big changes, so this suits him.
S0.do: Keeps the same shift and machine and holds on to two or three months of savings. Keeps chipping away at the mortgage as the family always has.
S0.feel: Fine and normal, with a little relief.
S0.fieldNote: Colin has already been forced into one career change by injury and treats stability as the main prize. He has never used AI and sees no reason to. His ambitions are modest and concrete, like a faster changeover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, companies will always go for cheaper. I wouldn't shout about it, there's no point. I'd say to the lads, keep your heads down and do a good job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the stacking and feeding is exactly what a robot arm does, and I'm the slowest one. I don't fancy my chances if they cut a shift. And my back means I can't go back to the warehouse even if they wanted me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try harder at the changeovers so I'm not the obvious one to go. I'd start putting more aside, maybe forty a week, and Tess might take more hours at the pharmacy. I wouldn't go on any computer courses, I'd just be the reliable one who turns up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, more than I'd let on at home. Knot in the stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody really. The bosses have to compete, the government can't stop it. It's like the weather, you just put your coat on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your savings are two or three months. What would you change about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop the Sky sports, which would hurt. Fewer takeaways. And no new car, the old Astra will have to keep going.

S1.say: It's business and companies will always go for cheaper, so there's no point shouting about it. He'd tell the lads to keep their heads down and do a good job.
S1.think: The stacking and feeding he does is exactly what a robot arm does, and he's the slowest. His back rules out going back to warehouse work, so he doesn't fancy his chances if a shift is cut.
S1.do: Works on his changeovers so he's not the obvious one to cut and saves about forty a week. Cancels the sports subscription and keeps the old car; his wife may take more pharmacy hours, but he avoids computer courses.
S1.feel: Worried, more than he'd admit at home, with a knot in his stomach.
S1.quote: It's like the weather, you just put your coat on.
S1.fieldNote: Colin doesn't blame anyone and treats the change as weather to be endured. His private fear is sharp, because his injury closes off his old fallback. His strategy is to be the dependable one rather than learn new skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that then, and I'd probably go quiet. It's not my thing to get on marches. I'd just say to Tess, we'll manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be out in the first year, along with half the plant. And what would there be for a bloke with a bad back and no qualifications? I don't know, and that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut everything back to the bone, no holidays, no extras, pay the mortgage first. I'd sign up for whatever the government offered and lean on Tess's parents if we had to. I'd look for anything going, security, driving, whatever didn't need my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's moving. I don't sleep well anyway, and I wouldn't sleep at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What happens in your house the week you hear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit down at the kitchen table, and Tess would do the sums because she's better at them. Ryan would ask if we're losing the house. I'd say no, and I'd hope I was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd just be reliable. Does that still work here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If the robot's cheaper, being reliable doesn't matter, the robot's reliable too. That's what gets me, there's nothing to be better at.

S2.say: Well, that's that, and he'd probably go quiet; marches aren't his thing. He'd tell his wife they'll manage.
S2.think: He'd likely be out in the first year with half the plant, and he can't see what's left for a man with a bad back and no qualifications. Not knowing frightens him.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the bone and pays the mortgage first. Signs up for any government help, leans on his wife's parents if needed and looks for work that doesn't strain his back, like security or driving.
S2.feel: Like the ground is moving, and he wouldn't sleep at all.
S2.quote: If the robot's cheaper, being reliable doesn't matter, the robot's reliable too.
S2.fieldNote: His only strategy, being the reliable one, collapses in the fast picture, and he says so plainly. He goes quiet publicly but privately expects to be out early. His son's question about the house is the moment that hit hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, it's coming and there's no stopping it. Maybe I'd say the government should help people retrain. Not much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't change the end, it just means I'd be 48 instead of 45 when it lands. The difference is the kids would be older. Ryan would be twenty, working himself, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder for the first few years, maybe sixty a week. Pay a bit extra on the mortgage when I can. I'd keep doing my job well and wait to see what the plant actually does before doing anything drastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried. Not panicking, but it'd sit there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Would the extra time change your mind about a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If it was something practical, like a forklift or a security licence, I'd do that. But not sitting at a computer learning stuff I'll never use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tess say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say we'll be fine, she always does, and she'd be the one who makes it fine. She'd probably have a spreadsheet by the weekend. I'd let her.

S3.say: It's coming and there's no stopping it, though maybe the government should help people retrain. He wouldn't say much more than that.
S3.think: Five years doesn't change the end, it just means he'd be 48 instead of 45 when it lands. The difference is his kids would be older, and his son might be working.
S3.do: Saves about sixty a week and pays extra on the mortgage when he can. Keeps doing his job well and waits to see what the plant does, open only to a practical licence like forklift or security.
S3.feel: Still worried, though not panicking; it would sit there in the background.
S3.quote: Not sitting at a computer learning stuff I'll never use.
S3.fieldNote: The extra years mainly matter to him because his children would be older, not because he'd do something new. He'd consider a practical licence but rejects anything screen-based. He relies heavily on his wife to manage the money side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so no need to panic. People panic and do daft things. I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is near enough to retirement for some, but not me, I'd be 53. Still, it's a long time, and by then I'd have caught up with the lads, so I wouldn't be first out the door. I'd hope to just ride it out until the last bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep saving a bit more each year. Maybe the forklift licence. And I'd make sure Ryan picks a trade that's harder for a robot, like his uncle's plumbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit easier. Like a bill that's not due for ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is there anything you'd do now that you wouldn't otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get Ryan into his uncle's plumbing firm, maybe, as an apprentice. That's the one thing I'd push. For me, I'd just keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you picture yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, no idea. Maybe still at the plant, watching the robots and fixing jams. Or on a security desk somewhere, if that's still a job.

S4.say: There's plenty of time, so there's no need to panic, because people who panic do daft things. He'd keep his head down.
S4.think: Ten years is a long time, and he'd hope to have caught up with his colleagues by then and ride it out. But at 53 he'd still be well short of retirement.
S4.do: Keeps working and saves a bit more each year, possibly getting a forklift licence. Pushes his son toward an apprenticeship at his uncle's plumbing firm.
S4.feel: A bit easier, like a bill that isn't due for ages.
S4.quote: Like a bill that's not due for ages.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline lets Colin fall back on his preferred approach of keeping going. His one active step is steering his son into a trade he thinks robots will reach late. The worry hasn't gone, it has just been pushed down the road.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. No time to save, and nothing for me to be better at. What would help is some money coming in while I find something, and someone telling me what jobs are left for a bloke who can't lift. Straight, without the jargon.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe that people like me don't make a fuss, so we get forgotten. My back went and nobody asked how I was coping, I just sorted it. I'd do the same again, but it'd be nice if someone asked first.

headlineQuote: People like me don't make a fuss, so we get forgotten.
portrait: Colin Hansen, 43, runs a rotary die-cutter at a cardboard box plant after a back injury ended sixteen years of loading lorries. He has never used AI, would rather ask a person, and treats change as weather to put a coat on for, blaming no one. In the mild pictures he is calm or quietly worried, planning only to be the reliable one, but fast AGI takes away even that and leaves him alarmed. More warning time mainly helps because his children would be older, and his one real plan is steering his son into plumbing.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to save and nothing he could become better at.
whatWouldHelp: Some income while he finds work, and plain advice without jargon on which jobs are left for someone who can't do heavy lifting.
